title: Meathook
author: Mark Rosenberg
desc:
The Meathook program is designed as a comprehensive, all-purpose training plan that integrates the personal training philosophies of Mark Rosenberg, and routines into a format that can be followed by the general lifting population. This program combines Mark's preferred weekly schedule, hypertrophy routines, and favorite progressions for strength development into a single, cohesive plan. While it offers a well-rounded approach to both size and strength gains, it is important to note that Meathook is not suitable for beginners. Intermediate and advanced lifters will find it challenging yet effective, as it caters to those with a solid foundation in training.

Meathook is not a specialized powerlifting or strength sport program, but it can be utilized in the off-season for athletes looking to build strength and size that will carry over to their sport-specific training. The 12-week program focuses on progressive overload and periodization to maximize muscle growth (hypertrophy) while also improving overall strength. It can be repeated indefinitely for consistent long-term progress.

For those who plan to run Meathook, access to a fully-equipped gym with a wide selection of machines is ideal, as this will optimize the hypertrophy-focused training days. However, the program can be adapted to work with a more minimal setup, though this may limit some aspects of the program's effectiveness, particularly on hypertrophy days. As with any comprehensive program, it is essential to read the entire document before starting to ensure you understand how to structure your training and get the most out of the program.

ex.note: 3-5 sets • At this point you should have one movement left. Here you can do something light and really high rep to burn out those muscles.
3-5 sets • Do not neglect these. Keep the work higher rep and smooth. The goal is to keep the tendons working and strong, as well as keep the wrists strong through their full range.
3-5 sets • I have found this to be the best movement to warm up the knees and get the legs ready for more work, without drastically impacting the following movements.

Squat movement • You can either build up to several, heavy, higher intensity sets, or you can perform a single set that makes you see god. Either way this should be the most challenging movement you do on a systemic level. If you go with several hard sets make sure you can maintain intensity through all of them, though the last should be really pushing you. If you go with a single set (and to be honest I think this is the ‘canon’ option) I want a hard set. 
• If you are only doing a single working set I want it to contain as much stimulus as a handful of regular working sets. It is mandatory to use intensity magnifiers on this set. These are techniques that let you push past traditional failure. Some example: 
- Rest pause reps: Take an extended pause at the top of each rep near the end to push more out, this should be on the magnitude of maybe 5-10 seconds tops, and the weight should be on your at all times.
- Cluster sets: take a short, fixed rest after a set then repeating that set as many times as you can. For example, perform 10 difficult reps, rest for 30 seconds (I suggest counting out loud or at least under your breath), then immediately perform the same set of 10. Keep doing this until you fail to get at least 5.
- Drop sets: Take a weight to failure, then immediately remove a portion of the weight and take that new weight to failure, repeat for a total of 3-5 drops.

After the intense squatting movement, and as long a break as you feel you need, I want you to find a more traditional leg press (or similar machine if you have options) and sit down for a couple sets of lighter weight higher reps. Use a stance/variation that lets you better isolate your legs (quads or glutes/hams depending on goals). The goal isn't to blast your whole system like the last movement. So feel free to take reps slower for ‘the burn’ not lock out at the top to maintain tension the whole set and take continuous reps so that your legs burnout before you or your willpower does. I like to use a close stance near the bottom of the footplate, with toes rotated way out to do ‘frog leg presses’ here, but your choice is going to depend on your goals and needs. But remember the goal is tired legs, not the feeling that you are going to leave your body on this one.

Quad isolation • These are just straight sets at a mid/high rep range again. Focus on isolating your quads. If you do choose to use a leg extension, try this fun finisher. Drop your weight to below half your working weight. Perform 5 reps using only one leg, then 5 reps using only the other leg. Repeat this switching off until you cannot. Then immediately take both legs and hit the same weight to absolute failure. Lots of fun.
3-5 sets • Here is where I program the calf work mostly just to give you a break before the last movement. Do whatever here, its calves, they don't really matter.

Optional exercise 3-5 sets • If you feel like your lower back is really pumped from anything you have already done, you can also add cable crunches here. They really stretch out the muscles and pull blood out, alleviating the feeling.

2-3 sets • Point is to have a hip dominant compound that doesn't have much knee flexion as your quads are not really in a place to help at this point. Here you will do 2-3 sets of 10ish, giving whatever you have left at this point.

3-5 sets • I have found this to be the best movement to warm up the knees and get the legs ready for more work, without drastically impacting the following movements.

Squat movement • You can either build up to several, heavy, higher intensity sets, or you can perform a single set that makes you see god. Either way this should be the most challenging movement you do on a systemic level. If you go with several hard sets make sure you can maintain intensity through all of them, though the last should be really pushing you. If you go with a single set (and to be honest I think this is the ‘canon’ option) I want a hard set. 
• If you are only doing a single working set I want it to contain as much stimulus as a handful of regular working sets. It is mandatory to use intensity magnifiers on this set. These are techniques that let you push past traditional failure. Some example: 
- Rest pause reps: Take an extended pause at the top of each rep near the end to push more out, this should be on the magnitude of maybe 5-10 seconds tops, and the weight should be on your at all times.
- Cluster sets: take a short, fixed rest after a set then repeating that set as many times as you can. For example, perform 10 difficult reps, rest for 30 seconds (I suggest counting out loud or at least under your breath), then immediately perform the same set of 10. Keep doing this until you fail to get at least 5.
- Drop sets: Take a weight to failure, then immediately remove a portion of the weight and take that new weight to failure, repeat for a total of 3-5 drops.

After the intense squatting movement, and as long a break as you feel you need, I want you to find a more traditional leg press (or similar machine if you have options) and sit down for a couple sets of lighter weight higher reps. Use a stance/variation that lets you better isolate your legs (quads or glutes/hams depending on goals). The goal isn't to blast your whole system like the last movement. So feel free to take reps slower for ‘the burn’ not lock out at the top to maintain tension the whole set and take continuous reps so that your legs burnout before you or your willpower does. I like to use a close stance near the bottom of the footplate, with toes rotated way out to do ‘frog leg presses’ here, but your choice is going to depend on your goals and needs. But remember the goal is tired legs, not the feeling that you are going to leave your body on this one.

Quad isolation • These are just straight sets at a mid/high rep range again. Focus on isolating your quads. If you do choose to use a leg extension, try this fun finisher. Drop your weight to below half your working weight. Perform 5 reps using only one leg, then 5 reps using only the other leg. Repeat this switching off until you cannot. Then immediately take both legs and hit the same weight to absolute failure. Lots of fun.
3-5 sets • Here is where I program the calf work mostly just to give you a break before the last movement. Do whatever here, its calves, they don't really matter.

Optional exercise 3-5 sets • If you feel like your lower back is really pumped from anything you have already done, you can also add cable crunches here. They really stretch out the muscles and pull blood out, alleviating the feeling.

2-3 sets • Point is to have a hip dominant compound that doesn't have much knee flexion as your quads are not really in a place to help at this point. Here you will do 2-3 sets of 10ish, giving whatever you have left at this point.
